"I wanted to be famous. I wanted to be a somebody". 17-year-old Marcus Sarjeant shoots blanks at the Queen of England. London. 1981

Marcus Simon Sarjeant (born 1964) fired six blank shots at Queen Elizabeth II as she rode down The Mall to the Trooping the Colour ceremony in 1981.

After leaving school in May 1980, Sarjeant applied to join the Royal Marines but could not accept the discipline and left after three months, claiming that officers bullied him. He also tried to join the Army but stayed only for two days of an induction course. His applications to join the police and the fire service were also dismissed.

After trying unsuccessfully to find ammunition for his father's revolver, Sarjeant purchased a starters pistol with blanks. He also sent a letter to Buckingham Palace which read "Your Majesty. Don't go to the Trooping the Colour ceremony because there is an assassin set up to kill you, waiting just outside the palace". The letter arrived on 16 June, three days after the incident.

On 13 June 1981, Sarjeant joined the crowds for Trooping the Colour. When the Queen came past riding her 19-year-old horse Burmese, Sarjeant quickly fired six blanks from his starting revolver. The horse was momentarily startled but the Queen brought her under control; she was unharmed. The soldier who closest to Sarjeant, grabbed him by the hair, pulled him over the crowd control barriers, disarmed him and wrestled him to the ground. Sarjeant told the soldiers "I wanted to be famous. I wanted to be a somebody" In particular he noted the ease with which Mark David Chapman had become famous after killing John Lennon.

Sarjeant was tried and found guilty of an offence under the Treason Act, sentencing him to five years' imprisonment, and was released after three years in jail which were mostly spent at Grendon Psychiatric Prison.
